They have no doubt realized that hosting third party models is far more profitable.

Let someone else take on the research and training costs, and charge a massive premium for your hardware.

There is intense competition in the AI industry, especially with AI firms in China driving down prices, so it seems likely that LLM's and software products may become fungible commodities that trade close to marginal cost = marginal revenue = minimum average total cost. In other words, most of the profits from AI and software development will be competed away, eventually.

Data center hardware, by contrast, is a scarce commodity with rapidly growing demand, and therefore likely to capture most of the profits from AI and software development, if current market conditions persist.

Today's IT business trends represent a remarkable change in the industry compared to the situation 50 years ago, when startups like Microsoft and Oracle, whose business models were based exclusively on software development, challenged and overthrew the dominant player, IBM, whose primary source of revenue was from hardware.

Notice that you also see Google really struggling (and falling behind) in the AI race. This, despite massive resources and being responsible for key pioneering research. Same reason why IBM has failed in this area. The big established companies tend to shut their brightest people into research departments where they write papers and produce demos while the main cash cow areas remain undisturbed, so they have collections of bright people and they have money, but they rarely let their brightest people make big bets with the money, whereas startups do.

I think this is Broken Window fallacy[0], though.

If a business can create software cheaper, then it can charge its customers less for that software (or, conversely, if a business can use an AI to create bespoke software for cheaper than it would cost to buy that software) then the customer business saves money. It, in turn, can use that money to improve its offering to its customers. They, in turn, and so on.

Having cheaper things means everyone gets more things. The value created is created further down the supply chain.

My suggestion to anybody staring this down is: do something for yourself while you can, while we're in the early going. Most people still have no understanding of AI, most tech employees are doing absolutely nothing interesting with it other than prompt prompt prompt prompt while at work and effectively doodling at home.

Go high value and go for the users. Do things that don't scale, that actually rings more true now than ever. Focus on areas of tech where it's really hard to get the users, where you have to practically hand acquire them to get started. Users are the moat.

It's not build the software and they will come. That's what nearly everybody has wrong about what is going on right now. The value is not in the software. Users, users, users, users - they should be your primary focus.

Also consider looking at software more as a layer related to something else you do, not as The Thing you do. Related to another service you offer, improving that service.

You read that it was a very wide open field, where the market was not yet highly concentrated, 3/4 of the market was mom & pop operators.
